newsitem.title: USA: Ford to boost output, add to profits.
newsitem.headline: Ford to boost output, add to profits.

text.p: As its rivals struggle with the aftermath of strikes, Ford Motor Co. said on Tuesday it plans to increase its scheduled second-quarter truck production, adding to what is already expected to be a record profit for the period.
The automaker is also considering a new sport utility vehicle that would be even bigger and more profitable than its monster Ford Expedition, industry analysts say.

Ford's stock closed at an all-time high of $38.125, up 87.5 cents on the New York Stock Exchange, on anticipation that Ford's second-quarter profits will likely exceed Wall Street's current consensus estimate of $2.04 billion, or $1.70 a share.
Ford's previous quarterly profit record was $1.9 billion in the second quarter of 1996.

"This week, we're going to add some truck production to our current second-quarter schedules," said Mel Stephens, Ford's investor relations manager. He added that the increase creates "the opportunity for profits to go up."
Like other automakers, Ford books sales and profits on vehicles as soon as they roll off the assembly line.

Merrill Lynch & Co. analyst Nicholas Lobaccaro said he is expecting Ford to increase second-quarter output by about 15,000 trucks, including Explorer sport utility vehicles and F-Series pickup trucks. He estimates Ford will earn $1.95 a share for the April-June period.
Also pushing Ford's profits forward are strong sales of its new full-size Expedition sport/utility vehicle, which sells for $35,000 to $40,000, with hefty profit margins.

In addition, Ford is achieving faster-than-anticipated cost cuts. It promised that it would reduce costs by $1 billion for the full 1997 year, but found $800 million in the first quarter alone. While the automaker cautioned that it could not sustain such a pace for the full year, many analysts believe it could double its $1 billion goal during 1997.

"I think things are coming along better than they had hoped," said Donald DeScenza, an independent auto analyst in New Canaan, Conn. "I think (cost cuts) will be over $2 billion and maybe as high as $2.5 billion for the year."

The Ford profit surge comes at a time when analysts have ratcheted back their earnings estimates for General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp., which have been hit by strikes that hurt production this year.
Salomon Brothers analyst Jack Kirnan on Tuesday cut his earnings estimate for Chrysler to 70 cents a share, or about $483 million, from 90 cents a share previously.

The Wall Street consensus estimate for Chrysler's second quarter is about $600 million, or 87 cents a share, according to First Call, which monitors industry analysts' earnings forecasts. Chrysler earned $1.04 billion, or $1.38 a share in the year-ago period.

In a research report, Kirnan said Chrysler's profitability is suffering from more than an engine plant strike that is expected to reduce second-quarter profits by $450 million. In addition, the automaker's incentive costs for minivans and other key vehicles are rising because of stiff competition during the spring selling season -- some of which is coming from Ford.
GM recently settled a car assembly plant strike in Oklahoma City, but an ongoing, six-week walkout at a truck plant in Pontiac, Mich., is continuing to siphon away profits.

Lehman Brothers analyst Joseph Phillippi said he plans to cut his second-quarter estimate for GM to $1.9 billion, or $2.45 a share, down from the Wall Street consensus of $2.60. GM earned $2.1 billion or $2.65 a share in the year-ago period.
The walkouts have cost GM more than $275 million in lost profits so far, Phillippi said.
Industry analysts say Ford is also considering a larger sport utility vehicle based on its new F-350 commercial pickup truck, which debuts this fall.

Ford declined to confirm plans for the vehicle, but an industry product analyst said the brawny sport utility, dubbed "Crew Wagon" within Ford, would be introduced in the 2000 or 2001 model year. It would be about 10 inches longer than the 18-foot Chevrolet Suburban and may feature six passenger doors -- four full-size doors plus two rear-hinged half-doors, much like those found on extended-cab pickup trucks.
It likely would be powered by a standard 5.4-litre V-8 engine and an optional 6.8-litre V-10 engine now available in Ford's Econoline van.
